A Tax With Cliffs

HAWAIʻI TAXES EVERY SALE OF REAL PROPERTY when the deed is recorded. The rate depends on the price and applies to the whole of it, so the tax jumps at each threshold: a home that sells for $3,999,000 pays 0.5 percent, or $19,995, and one that sells for $4,000,000 pays 0.7 percent, or $28,000. Buyers who cannot claim a county homeowner exemption, because the home will not be their main residence, pay a slightly higher schedule (Table 1).1

The tax raised $96 million in fiscal year 2025.2 The first 10 percent, up to $5.1 million, goes to the land conservation fund and half, up to $38 million, to the rental housing revolving fund. The rest goes to the general fund.3

Today’s rate applies to the whole price of a sale in the band. The draft’s rate applies only to the part of the price within the band, and the total is capped at 4 percent of the price for owner-occupants and 6 percent for other buyers. Today’s owner-occupant schedule also covers commercial, agricultural and other nonresidential property, and the draft keeps it for them.

What SB 3028 Would Change

THE LAST DRAFT OF SB 3028 would tax home sales the way the income tax taxes income: each rate applies only to the part of the price within its band.4 For a buyer who will live in the home, the part of the price between $2 million and $3 million would be taxed at 2 percent and the part between $3 million and $6 million at 4 percent. For other buyers, those rates would be 5 percent and 7 percent. The band edges would rise each year with consumer prices, starting in 2027. Nonresidential property would stay on today’s schedule.

Because the rates below $2 million would change little and apply only to each slice of the price, the draft cuts the tax on every owner-occupied sale under $2,247,000 and every other home sale under $2,073,000. Above those prices it raises the tax, steeply (Table 2). House Finance Committee Chair Chris Todd gave the same thresholds, about $2.3 million and $2.1 million, when his committee approved the draft on April 2, 2026.5

House and Senate negotiators met through May 1 without agreeing, and the bill died with the session.6 The draft is the fullest statement of where the Legislature left the idea, and the model scores its rates as written, as if enacted in 2027.

Who Would Pay More

MOST SALES WOULD PAY THE SAME OR LESS. Maui is the one county that publishes every sale with its price and the conveyance tax paid.7 Of its sales in recent years, 43 percent would pay less under the draft and 42 percent the same, mostly because they are nonresidential or sell for less than $600,000. The other 15 percent would pay more. Chair Todd put the statewide share paying the same or less at 91 percent; Maui’s is lower because it has more expensive homes than the rest of the state, relative to its size (Table 4).

Nearly all of the new revenue would come from the top of the market. On Maui, sales above $4 million would provide 88 percent of it, and buyers who will not make the home their main residence 90 percent. Statewide the share is about the same, 89 percent. Even on Oʻahu, where most homes worth $2 million or more are lived in by their owners, those homes sell less often than second homes and rentals, and their buyers pay the lower owner-occupant rates.

The $3 Million to $4 Million Home

A HOME SELLING FOR $3.5 MILLION to a family that will live in it pays $17,500 in conveyance tax today. Under the draft it would pay $46,300. Sold to anyone else, it would pay $93,800 instead of $21,000. This is where the draft turns steep: at $3 million the rate on each added dollar jumps to 4 percent for owner-occupants and 7 percent for other buyers, while today’s rate holds at 0.5 or 0.6 percent of the price up to $4 million.

At fiscal year 2028 prices, about 71 Maui homes a year sell for $3 million to $4 million, 52 of them to buyers who will not live in them. Those buyers’ average tax would rise from $20,549 to $84,073. For owner-occupants it would rise from $16,892 to $38,796. Even so, the band provides only 10 percent of Maui’s new revenue, because far more money changes hands above it (Figure 1).

The draft also ends today’s cliff at $4 million. Under it, a sale at $3,999,000 and one at $4,000,000 would owe almost the same, $66,260 and $66,300 for an owner-occupant, where today they differ by $8,005. These are the amounts due at the sale; part of a tax on sales can be passed back to sellers through the price.

What It Would Raise

STATEWIDE, THE DRAFT WOULD RAISE an estimated $70 million more than current law in fiscal year 2028, the first full year a bill passed in 2027 could reach. That is on top of about $116 million the tax would raise anyway. Before accounting for fewer sales, the increase would be $115 million.8

Transfer taxes discourage sales. Toronto’s 1.1 percent land transfer tax cut sales of single-family homes by about 15 percent,9 and a 1-point cut in the United Kingdom’s transaction tax raised short-run sales activity by about 20 percent.10 The estimates assume sales fall 10 percent for each point of the price the draft adds in tax, and rise where it cuts the tax. A response of 5 to 15 percent instead gives $53 million to $90 million.

Maui County would provide $22 million and Oʻahu $22 million, though Maui has only 14 percent of the state’s home sales by value to Oʻahu’s 62 percent. The difference is who owns the expensive homes. Of Maui’s 6,472 homes worth $2 million or more, 69 percent are not lived in by their owners; of Oʻahu’s 15,012, 38 percent. Second homes and rentals sell more often and pay the higher rates (Figure 3 and Table 4).

Revenue grows faster than home prices, because as prices rise, more of each sale falls in the higher bands. Indexing the bands to consumer prices slows this but does not stop it while home prices rise faster, as the model assumes (4 percent a year against 3 percent). By fiscal year 2031 the increase reaches $76 million (Figure 4).

Checking against the House. Chair Todd said the draft would raise about $20 million a year less than the roughly $170 million of the House’s original proposal, which puts it near $150 million.5 The House’s method is not public. Scored the same way, without a change in sales and at 2023 to 2026 prices, this estimate comes to $91 million. A figure near $150 million follows if the other three counties together have about 4 times Maui’s expensive homes, in proportion to the conveyance tax each pays now. Parcel records show Oʻahu and Hawaiʻi Island together with 1.7 times Maui’s count of homes worth $2 million or more that their owners do not live in.

Where the Money Would Go

THE DRAFT ALSO REWRITES who gets the money. Before any reaches the general fund, it would send 5 percent, up to $10 million, to the land conservation fund; 20 percent, up to $40 million, to the rental housing revolving fund; 30 percent, up to $60 million, to the Hawaiian home lands infrastructure and housing special fund; and 20 percent, up to $40 million, to transit-oriented development infrastructure.4

Those shares add up to 75 percent of all conveyance tax, including the tax on sales the draft leaves unchanged, until the funds reach their caps. The general fund therefore comes out ahead only if the draft raises more than about $107 million a year, more than this estimate. In fiscal year 2028 the general fund would receive $46 million, $26 million less than under current law, while the four funds together would receive $139 million. Even at the top of the range, the general fund would receive $17 million less (Table 7).

How These Estimates Are Made

BECAUSE TODAY’S TWO SCHEDULES DIFFER, the tax recorded on a Maui sale shows which one applied, and so whether the buyer could claim a homeowner exemption. Of sales with a price and tax in fiscal years 2023 to 2026, 97 percent match one schedule to within half a percent; the rest are treated as nonresidential, whose tax the draft leaves alone. The county’s land-use codes separate owner-occupied homes from nonresidential property on the owner-occupant schedule. Applied to the sorted home sales, current law reproduces the tax Maui recorded on them to within a few hundred dollars a year. The model uses about 2,680 sales a year in all.7

No other county publishes its sales with prices, so the other three are built from Maui’s. Joining every Maui sale to the county’s assessment listing shows how often homes of each assessed value sell, split by whether their owners live in them, which kind of buyer bought them, and at what price relative to the assessment. Oʻahu and Hawaiʻi Island publish the same kind of records home by home: the City’s assessment tables, which list every parcel and condominium unit with its value and exemptions,11 and Hawaiʻi County’s parcel records, whose condominium projects are split into units by their unit counts.12 Applying Maui’s rates to those homes gives each county’s sales by price, which are then scored like Maui’s. Buildings of five or more units are left out of the rates and the counts, as are records worth $20 million or more that are not condominium units or known single homes, since most are apartment or resort properties. Applied to Maui’s own homes, the same rates recover 74 percent of Maui’s increase, because they also leave out sales at nominal prices, new construction and vacant lots, so the other two counties are scaled up to match. The key assumption is that homes of a given value and occupancy sell as often, and to the same kinds of buyers, as on Maui. Kauaʻi publishes no values by parcel, so its increase scales Maui’s by the value above $2 million on its property tax roll and in the American Community Survey.

Two checks. On Oʻahu the model finds about 456 sales a year of $2 million or more at recent prices, against 286 single-family homes alone in the multiple listing service, before condominiums and unlisted sales.15 Rebuilt from those listed sales instead, Oʻahu’s increase before any change in sales is $25 million to $43 million, depending on how the unlisted sales in new condominium towers are priced, around this estimate’s $34 million. Across all prices, the model finds fewer home sales on Oʻahu and Hawaiʻi Island than the Bureau of Conveyances records (7,783 against 10,781 a year on Oʻahu),16 mostly among new and lower-priced homes, where the draft changes little. Sales of apartment buildings with five or more units are scored under the draft’s rule that sets the rate by the price per unit, which lowers their tax; on Maui there were 17 such sales in four years. Left out: long-term leases, a rush of sales before the law takes effect, and any effect on prices. The sales behind the estimate, from 2023 to 2026, came in a slow market: the tax raised about $95 million a year then, against $188 million in fiscal year 2022. In a stronger market both the tax and the increase would be larger. The full method and every parameter are in the source code.8

This page was revised on September 25, 2026 to build the statewide estimate county by county. The first version scaled Maui’s results up by the conveyance tax each county group paid and gave $69 million to $118 million after fewer sales; a first revision, scaling by each county’s value above $2 million on its tax roll, gave $67 million (Table 8).
